paper_a.title: Limit Laws for Random Matrices and Free Products

paper_b.title: Distribution of Eigenvalues for Some Sets of Random Matrices

metadata.description: Voiculescu (1991) recasts and substantially extends classical RMT. The Marcenko-Pastur (1967) theorem on empirical spectra of A_N + sum tau_i q q^* (and its named density for sums of independent rank-one projections) is recovered in Voiculescu's framework as a multiplicative free convolution of the Gaussian X^*X distribution with a projection-distributed measure (paper A's Example in section 3.6). Where MP67 derives the limit Stieltjes transform from a self-consistent integral/PDE built one rank-one perturbation at a time, Voiculescu identifies the limit operator-algebraically with free creation/annihilation operators on the Fock space, and proves asymptotic freeness of independent Gaussian, Haar-unitary, and Grassmannian-projection ensembles. The two papers therefore share the same limiting object (semicircle and MP densities) but differ fundamentally in machinery (free probability vs. resolvent / Stieltjes-transform analysis); the relation is EXT with paper A extending paper B's setting to a unified non-commutative-probability framework.

matches.explanation: Both define the basic random self-adjoint object built from rank-one projections. Paper A's DP325.10 is the family of independent uniformly distributed projections on Grassmannians G_{n,k_j}, while paper B's DP326.1 builds B_N(n) = A_N + sum tau_i q^(i)(., q^(i)) — a deterministic operator plus a sum of independent rank-one (projection-times-coefficient) operators. Paper A treats the projections themselves as the primary random objects (and the coefficients enter through free convolution with a scalar measure), while paper B parametrises the same construction by (q^(i), tau_i) with q^(i) random unit vectors. Same physical setup, different algebraic packaging.

Paper A's DP325.7 sets up the algebra M_n of n x n random matrices with the normalised expected trace varphi_n = E[tr/n] — this is the ambient probability space inside which limits are taken. Paper B uses the empirical spectral function nu(lambda; B_N(n)) = #{eigenvalues < lambda}/N (DP326.2) on a similar matrix-valued random object (DP326.1). The two are the operator-algebraic vs. measure-theoretic encodings of the same data: moments under varphi_n equal moments of the empirical spectral measure.

The non-commutative probability space, free family, free random variables, joint distribution functional and asymptotic-freeness/limit distribution are paper A's defining contributions and have no counterpart in paper B (1967), which works entirely within classical resolvent / Stieltjes-transform analysis. These are the central novelties that justify EXT as the pair-level relation.

Additive and multiplicative free convolution (boxplus, boxtimes) are paper A's core operations. Paper B has no analogue: it computes the limit Stieltjes transform from the self-consistent integral equation (1.14) directly, not by convolving sub-distributions. The closest thing in paper B is the implicit characteristic representation of TP326.2, but that is a single PDE, not a binary operation on distributions.

The full Fock space and creation operators l_j realise free semicircular variables on a concrete Hilbert space. This is the Hilbert-space model that paper A uses to identify limit objects of Gaussian random matrices (TP325.5); paper B has no Fock-space construction.

Standard family of independent Haar unitaries — paper A's setting for TP325.6 and TP325.7. Paper B's TP326.3 does treat random unitary matrices, but parameterised differently (V_N times a product of single-projection rotations e^{i r(k/n)}), not as a single Haar-distributed family.

Both nodes state the semicircle law as the limit eigenvalue distribution of suitably normalised sums (paper A: free CLT for sums of free centered variables; paper B: cited Wigner theorem for Gaussian symmetric matrices). The semicircle density (1/(2 pi)) sqrt(4 - lambda^2) on [-2, 2] in paper B coincides with paper A's TP325.1 in the standard normalisation. Both nodes carry origin = external (TP325.1 cites Voiculescu's earlier work; TP326.4 cites Wigner) so this match is informative as a structural anchor for the pair-level relation but does not by itself signal A->B novelty.

Paper A's TP325.3 (asymptotic freeness of independent self-adjoint Gaussian random matrices, with semicircle marginals) directly contains Wigner's law as a special case (one matrix). Paper B states Wigner's law (TP326.4) and explains in RP326.1 how the c -> infinity limit of the MP density of Example 1 reduces to Wigner's semicircle via the central limit theorem. Same conclusion (semicircle for normalised Gaussian/projection sums), but TP325.3 is much stronger: it produces semicircle limits AND asymptotic freeness across multiple independent Gaussian matrices and constant diagonals — a multivariate result that paper B does not prove.

This is the central content match. Paper A's ExP325.3 (rectangular Gaussian matrix, projection special case) derives psi_{mu boxtimes nu}(z) = (1 - z(beta+1) + sqrt((z(1-beta)-1)^2 - 4 beta z))/(2 z), which is the Stieltjes-transform form of the Marcenko-Pastur density supported on [tau(1-sqrt c)^2, tau(1+sqrt c)^2]. Paper B's TP326.1 is the original Marcenko-Pastur theorem giving exactly this density via the self-consistent equation, and ExP326.1 makes the density explicit as d nu/d lambda = sqrt(4 c tau^2 - (lambda - c tau - tau)^2)/(2 pi c tau lambda) (plus point mass (1-c) delta(lambda) for c<1). The two formulas describe the same measure under the substitution beta <-> c. PDF-fallback caveat noted: both papers' LaTeX is paraphrased, but the formulas line up unambiguously by name and structure, hence exact at confidence high.

ExP325.2 computes the limit distribution of Z^* Z = D^* X^* X D for Gaussian X and constant diagonal D as mu boxtimes nu via the S-transform identity S_{mu boxtimes nu} = S_mu S_nu. Paper B's TP326.1 + EP326.1 produce the limit spectrum of B_N(n) = A_N + sum tau_i P_i (a deterministic + projection-weighted-by-tau model) via the self-consistent Stieltjes equation. The two compute the same kind of object (limit spectrum of a 'twisted projection sum') by different machinery: free multiplicative convolution / S-transform vs. fixed-point Stieltjes equation. Paper A explicitly notes that this recovers, by free-convolution methods, results obtained combinatorially in Wachter — a direct manifestation of EXT.

Both packages are the analytic transform that turns the limit-distribution problem into a tractable algebraic equation. Paper A's S-transform S_mu = chi_mu(z) z^{-1}(1+z) linearises multiplicative free convolution. Paper B's Stieltjes transform m(z; c) = int d nu(lambda)/(lambda - z) and its self-consistent equation EP326.1 m(z; c)(z + c int (x d sigma)/(1 + x m)) = -1 directly characterises the limit measure. Different transforms (S vs. Stieltjes) but the same role: closed-form analytic handle on the limit distribution. EP325.1 is external (cited from Voiculescu) so it primarily anchors the analytic-machinery comparison.

Free CLT under second-order freeness conditions is paper A's main combinatorial-style theorem reducing asymptotic freeness to moment-vanishing conditions. Paper B has no such generalised second-order-condition theorem — it works directly with the rank-one perturbation chain.

Asymptotic freeness for the GOE / antisymmetric Gaussian pair is paper-A original. Paper B is restricted to the rank-one-projection-plus-coefficient model and does not treat real-symmetric Gaussian ensembles as a separate case.

Identification of general (non-self-adjoint) Gaussian random matrices' *-distribution limit with creation+annihilation operators T_j = l_{2j-1} + l_{2j}^* on the Fock space is paper A's flagship operator-algebraic statement. Paper B has no concept of *-distribution for non-Hermitian matrices and no Fock-space realisation.

Both treat random unitary matrices but in very different ways. Paper A's TP325.6 says independent Haar-distributed unitaries are asymptotically free with each other and with any constant unitary, with marginal Haar limit on T. Paper B's TP326.3 computes the limit spectral function of U_N(n) = V_N prod_k [(I-P_k) + P_k exp(i r(k/n))] (a product of single-projection rotations driven by a continuous profile r). Same broad subject (asymptotic spectra of random unitary matrices), but the constructions and conclusions differ; paper A is multivariate / freeness, paper B is univariate / one-PDE.

Concentration of words in independent Haar unitaries (mu_n(D_n^epsilon(g)) -> 1) is paper-A original and uses the Levy-family / Gromov-Milman machinery. Paper B has no concentration / Levy-family component.

Asymptotic freeness of independent Grassmannian projections is paper-A original. Paper B uses random projections (in the q^(i) q^(i)* form) as building blocks but never asks whether several independent such projections are mutually free — that very question requires the free-probability vocabulary that paper B predates.
Fermionic CAR analogue of TP325.3 — paper-A original; paper B has no fermionic component.

Both are the 'recover Wigner' moment within the larger paper. Paper A's ExP325.1 specialises Theorems 2.2/2.3 to the complex/real Gaussian self-adjoint case to recover the semicircle. Paper B's RP326.1 takes the c -> infinity limit of MP Example 1 and notes it reduces to Wigner's semicircle via the CLT. Same Wigner-recovery role, different mechanisms.

Composite proof-vs-proof entry. Paper A's proofs (PP325.1-PP325.7) follow a moment-method / combinatorial pairings + reduction-to-free-CLT pattern (see proof_steps PSP325.1-11), with key ingredients: bounding mixed moments by counting pairings of order 2 without fixed points, and reducing asymptotic freeness to the free CLT. Paper B's PP326.1 (Haar uniqueness method) and PP326.2 (chain construction + compactness + identification + uniqueness + truncation; PSP326.1-11) instead build the limit by adding rank-one perturbations one at a time and identifying the limit Stieltjes transform via a self-consistent integral equation. Both are the central proof scaffolds of their papers; the explanation for grouping them as one analogous match is that they prove fundamentally connected limit-spectrum results by genuinely different techniques. Per v2 rules, individual proof_step <-> proof_step matches are not emitted.

The concentration ratio c = lim n/N is the central asymptotic regime parameter in paper B. Paper A operates in the n -> infinity limit of n x n matrices without a separate 'aspect ratio' parameter, except in the rectangular-matrix example (ExP325.3) where beta plays the same role. The MP67 ratio c is structurally tied to paper B's operator construction; paper A's framework absorbs it into the projection rank fraction.

Paper B's standing Conditions I-IV (ratio limit, A_N spectral limit, q-vector moment conditions, i.i.d. tau) are technical hypotheses specific to its rank-one-perturbation analysis. Paper A's hypotheses are operator-algebraic (trace state, freeness, normalisation) and do not factor into a similar finite list; no clean counterpart.

Quantile tau(xi), empirical distribution sigma(x, T_n) and its inverse tau(xi, T_n), and the auxiliary interpolant u(z, xi; N, T_n, Q_n) are all proof-scaffolding constructions internal to paper B's chain-perturbation argument. They have no role in paper A's proofs.

The edge equation (1.16) and singularity exponent formula (1.17) describe square-root (and higher-order) edge behaviour of the limit density. Paper A computes specific densities (e.g. semicircle and the MP-type formula in ExP325.3) whose edges are visible from the closed forms, but does not prove a general edge-singularity theorem.

Theorem 2 of MP67 generalises Theorem 1 to a continuous coefficient profile r(t). Paper A's framework would in principle absorb such a generalisation as a free convolution against a measure with density determined by r, but no specific corresponding theorem is stated in paper A.

Paper B's five lemmas — quadratic-form concentration (LP326.1), rank-one resolvent perturbation identity (LP326.2), L^1 convergence of the empirical quantile (LP326.3), mean-zero of the auxiliary functional (LP326.4), and Haar-style uniqueness for the integral equation (LP326.5) — are technical pillars of its specific proof technique (chain of rank-one perturbations + Stieltjes interpolant + uniqueness). Paper A uses entirely different infrastructure (combinatorial pairings + free CLT + Fock-space identification), so none of these lemmas have direct counterparts.
